name: Zane Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right. I'll be straight with you, I don't trust surveys much. But my nan always said if someone asks your opinion, give it to them properly. So here I am.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an offsider, which means a helper, on a jumbo at the Granite Hill nickel mine, underground. The jumbo's the drill rig with the big arms that drills the face so the charge-up crew can blast it. My job is helping the operator, Wes: changing drill bits, running the water and power lines, scaling loose rock off the back with a bar, and learning to drive it when he lets me. I'm still slow, Wes does in ten minutes what takes me thirty. My grandad and my dad both worked this ground, so it feels like the family trade. What wears me out is the heat at the bottom levels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying all along, it's a lot of noise from people in city offices who've never been underground. I don't post online, but I'd say it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I learn the jumbo, get my ticket, and do what Dad did. That's all I've ever wanted, a fair day's pay for putting holes in rock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just keep going. Learn from Wes, get signed off on the jumbo in the next year or so, keep putting money aside. Kayla and I are hoping to buy a little place near her mum's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's the world as it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any of the AI tools now, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Kayla uses something to write captions for her salon's page. I don't see the point. If I need to know something, I ask Wes or Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, "See? Same as the last ten things they said would change everything." He's been through a few of those.

S0.say: I'd say it's what I've said all along, a lot of noise from people in city offices who've never been underground. I'd say it at the pub rather than online.
S0.think: Privately it means I learn the jumbo, get my ticket and do what my dad did. That's all I've ever wanted: fair pay for drilling rock.
S0.do: Keeps learning from his operator Wes and aims to be signed off on the jumbo within about a year. Keeps saving towards a small place near his partner Kayla's mother.
S0.feel: Calm, as if the world is as it should be.
S0.quote: That's all I've ever wanted, a fair day's pay for putting holes in rock.
S0.fieldNote: Family tradition is the centre of his identity, three generations on the same ground. He doesn't use AI and doesn't see why he would, preferring to ask people he trusts. His distrust of city offices came up within the first minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck automating the bottom of Granite Hill. It's hot, wet and the ground moves. The machines they've got now can't handle half of what we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know they've got jumbos that drill the face on their own already, set up from the surface. Wes has seen one at another mine. So maybe it's me who's kidding himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working. I'm not going to chase some course for a job that might not exist. If the mine changed things, I'd see what they offered then. I'd hang on to the savings, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like it, but I don't think it's tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You just said maybe you're kidding yourself. What would it take to convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw one running here. Not a video, not a brochure. If I saw a jumbo drill a round at Granite Hill with no one in the seat, I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think pushes these changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tech companies selling to head office, and head office trying to please shareholders. And the government, with all the safety paperwork, makes it cheaper to have a machine than a man. It's not the guys on site asking for it.

S1.say: I'd say good luck automating the bottom of Granite Hill, which is hot, wet and moving. The machines they have now can't handle half of what we do.
S1.think: Privately he knows self-drilling jumbos already exist at other mines, set up from the surface. He admits he might be kidding himself.
S1.do: Keeps his head down, keeps working and holds onto his savings. Won't chase a course for a job that may not exist and will wait to see what the mine offers.
S1.feel: Uneasy, disliking it but not expecting it soon.
S1.quote: If I saw a jumbo drill a round at Granite Hill with no one in the seat, I'd believe it.
S1.fieldNote: He named the gap between his public line and private knowledge himself. Only seeing a driverless jumbo on his own ground would convince him. He blames tech sellers, head office and government safety rules, not the people on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let tech companies run the country. I'd vote out whoever let it happen. And I'd tell people to look after their own, because no one else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be finished. I've got one trade, and I'm not even fully trained in it yet. My dad would lose his job too, and Kayla's salon would lose customers when everyone's out of work. Two years isn't time to do anything except hang on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house savings and keep it as a safety net. Sell the boat Dad and I share, cut back on everything. If the job went, we'd move in with Kayla's mum and I'd help my uncle on his farm for board, at least till robots take that too. I'd lean on family and church, that's what they're there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm being honest. Angry first, then scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family and church are what they're there for. What would the church do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our pastor runs a food hamper thing already for people who are struggling. I've helped pack them. I never thought I'd be on the other side of that table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government support, if it was on offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. But if it's a choice between that and Kayla going without, I'd take it and keep my mouth shut about it. I'd rather it was work, though, even digging fence holes.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when tech companies run the country, and I'd vote out whoever let it happen. I'd tell people to look after their own.
S2.think: Privately he'd be finished, with one half-learned trade, his dad's job gone too and his partner's salon losing customers. Two years is only time to hang on.
S2.do: Stops the house savings to keep a safety net and sells the boat he shares with his dad. If the job goes, moves in with his partner's mother, works on his uncle's farm for board and leans on family and church.
S2.quote: I never thought I'd be on the other side of that table.
S2.fieldNote: His anger turned quickly to fear when he pictured his whole family's income at once. The image of moving from packing church hampers to receiving one hit him hard. He would accept government help but only quietly and as a last resort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to make the government protect local jobs. Put limits on it, make companies keep people on. I'd be talking to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years... I'd probably get my ticket, do two or three good years on the jumbo and then get pushed out. I'm not sure I'd do anything differently in the first year, to be honest. That's my nature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and save harder, no boat trips, no new truck. I'd vote for whoever promises to stand up for mining towns, and I'd go to a meeting if someone organised one. Otherwise I'd see what happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like hearing a creak in the back and not knowing if it'll hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you probably wouldn't do anything different. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Kayla would tell me to get moving. But I've watched people chase every new thing and end up with nothing. I'd rather be good at one thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'a creak in the back' mean for someone who's never been underground?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The back's the roof of the tunnel. When the rock's moving it groans, a sort of crack and creak. You learn to listen to the ground, and this picture sounds like the ground's moving.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to make the government protect local jobs, with limits on automation and rules that make companies keep people on. I'd talk to anyone who'd listen.
S3.think: Privately he'd probably get his ticket, have two or three good years on the jumbo and then be pushed out. He doubts he'd change anything in the first year.
S3.do: Keeps working and saves harder, skipping boat trips and a new truck. Votes for whoever promises to stand up for mining towns and goes to a meeting if one is organised, otherwise waits.
S3.feel: Anxious, like hearing the roof creak and not knowing if it'll hold.
S3.quote: You learn to listen to the ground, and this picture sounds like the ground's moving.
S3.fieldNote: His trade language is vivid, and the creaking roof was the clearest way he could describe dread. Five years makes him want government protection, even though he otherwise prefers free markets. He openly expects not to change his own course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and they'll have found ten new problems by then. People were saying the mine would close when I was in primary school, and it's still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get a good run out of it. Ten years, I'd be thirty-seven, a proper operator, maybe a house. The Lord's got a plan, and I'm not going to lose sleep over 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different in the first year. Get my ticket, get on the jumbo, keep saving for the house. Maybe in a few years I'd look at what the younger guys are doing, but I'd see first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's far enough off that it doesn't feel real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're very calm here, but you were scared in the fast one. Is it the time, or do you not believe it'll happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, if I'm honest. Ten years out, I'll believe it when I see it. Ask me again when there's a robot in the lunch room eating my sandwiches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had kids by then, would you want them going underground?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to have the choice. Dad gave me that. I'd hate to be the generation that has nothing to hand down.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and they'll find ten new problems by then. People said the mine would close when I was in primary school and it's still here.
S4.think: Privately he'd get a good run of ten years and be a proper operator with maybe a house by thirty-seven. He trusts God's plan and won't lose sleep over 2036.
S4.do: Changes nothing in the first year: gets his jumbo ticket, works and keeps saving for a house. Might look at what younger workers are doing in a few years but would wait first.
S4.feel: Calm, because it's too far off to feel real.
S4.quote: Ask me again when there's a robot in the lunch room eating my sandwiches.
S4.fieldNote: His calm here rests partly on not believing it will happen, which he admitted when pressed. Faith and family tradition carry him. The fear of having nothing to hand down to his own children was the one crack in the calm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is the government making mines keep local people on, and real apprenticeships, paid, for proper trades. Not a cheque in the mail, a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. A man who works hard and gets told he's not needed, that does something to him that money doesn't fix.

headlineQuote: A man who works hard and gets told he's not needed, that does something to him that money doesn't fix.
portrait: Zane Torres is 27 and works as an offsider on a jumbo drill rig at the Granite Hill nickel mine, the third generation of his family to work that ground. He lives with his partner Kayla, a hairdresser, and is saving for a small place near her mother's. He never uses AI, prefers to ask people he trusts, and blames tech companies, head office and government red tape for pushing automation. He's calm in the plateau, uneasy with steady change, alarmed and angry when AGI comes in two years, and calm again at ten years, partly because he doesn't believe it will happen.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his whole family's income could go at once with no time to do anything but hang on.
whatWouldHelp: Rules making mines keep local people on, and paid apprenticeships for proper trades, meaning a job rather than a cheque in the mail.
